overview:
Gommatasara is a seminal Digambara Jain scripture composed by Acharya Nemichandra Siddhānta‑Chakravarti (c. 10th–11th century CE). It is regarded as a concise, systematized presentation (sāra, “essence”) of earlier, voluminous doctrinal works—especially the Śaṭkhaṇḍāgama and its commentary Dhavalā—on the nature of the soul (jīva) and karma. The title “Gommatasara” is traditionally linked to the patron Chamundarāya, whose childhood name “Gommaṭa” and the colossal image of Gommateśvara at Śravaṇa Beḷgoḷa gave the work its name: the ‘essence’ prepared for Gommaṭa.

The text is divided into two major sections: Jīva‑kāṇḍa (the section on the soul) and Karma‑kāṇḍa (the section on karma). Jīva‑kāṇḍa presents a highly structured taxonomy of living beings and their spiritual progression. It expounds the fourteen guṇasthānas (spiritual stages), multiple classifications of souls (jīva‑samāsa), vitalities (prāṇa), capacities for development (paryāpti), and a set of fourteen “soul‑quests” (mārgana) that analyze the soul from different doctrinal angles such as senses, embodiment, passions, knowledge, control, and capacity for liberation. Karma‑kāṇḍa, in turn, offers a technical exposition of karmic matter, its varieties (prakṛti), modes of bondage, duration, intensity, fruition, and the processes of karmic inflow (āsrava), bondage (bandha), subsidence (upaśama), and destruction (kṣaya).

In terms of presentation, Gommatasara is composed in Prakrit gāthās (verses) with a dense, aphoristic style, designed to be unpacked by commentaries and oral teaching. Each doctrinal topic is introduced, defined, and then elaborated through numerical classifications and logical distinctions. The Jīva‑kāṇḍa moves from the general—what a soul is and how it is distinct from the body—to increasingly fine‑grained categories: one‑sensed to five‑sensed beings, mobile and immobile, group‑souled (nigoda) and individual‑souled, rational and irrational, capable and incapable of liberation. The Karma‑kāṇḍa similarly proceeds from basic definitions of karma to intricate tables of how specific karmas bind in particular spiritual stages and conditions.

Gommatasara’s presentation is deeply intertwined with the Jain doctrine of guṇasthāna. The fourteen stages—from mithyātva (deluded belief) through various degrees of right faith, right conduct, and passion‑reduction up to kevala‑jñāna (omniscience) and mokṣa—are used as a backbone for organizing both soul‑classification and karma‑analysis. The text shows how changes in the soul’s thought‑activity (bhāva) and vibratory activity (yoga) lead to different karmic inflows and transformations, thereby mapping spiritual psychology onto a precise karmic physics.

Historically, Gommatasara stands as one of the core Digambara doctrinal compendia, alongside works like Labdhisāra, Kṣaṇasāra, and Trilokasāra, also attributed to Nemichandra. It became a central text for later Digambara scholasticism and is frequently cited in commentarial literature. Modern printed editions and translations—such as J. L. Jaini’s English translation of Jīva‑kāṇḍa and the critical editions of Karma‑kāṇḍa by A. N. Upadhye and Kailash Chandra Shastri—have further shaped how the text is presented to contemporary students: often with extensive introductions explaining its relation to Śaṭkhaṇḍāgama, its numerical schemes, and its role in the technical study of karma and guṇasthāna.

From a pedagogical perspective, Gommatasara’s presentation is both systematic and demanding. It assumes familiarity with core Jain categories (jīva, ajīva, karma, guṇasthāna, lesyā, etc.) and then refines them through elaborate classifications. For advanced study, it serves as a bridge between narrative or ethical expositions of Jainism and the highly technical doctrinal tradition. For lay readers, modern summaries often highlight key themes—such as the centrality of consciousness, the moral significance of passions, and the possibility of liberation—while leaving the more intricate numerical and karmic tables to specialized study. Because of its density and its reliance on earlier canonical material, serious engagement with Gommatasara is usually undertaken under the guidance of qualified teachers and with reference to both traditional commentaries and modern scholarship.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara Jīva‑kāṇḍa
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhānta‑Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
णाणदंसणचरित्तसुद्धि‑लहाओ जिवो मुक्को होइ ।
जिवो देहसम्बन्धो देहस्स उवयाओ न होइ तं ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇāṇa‑damsaṇa‑caritta‑suddhi‑lahāo jivo mukko hoi;
jivo deha‑sambandho dehassa uvayāo na hoi taṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
The soul, attaining purity of knowledge, faith, and conduct, becomes liberated.
The soul is related to the body, yet it is not a modification of the body.
primary_sources.notes: These verses illustrate two core themes of Jīva‑kāṇḍa’s presentation: liberation as the perfection of knowledge, faith, and conduct, and the ontological distinction between soul and body. The text repeatedly emphasizes that while the soul is empirically associated with bodily states, its essential nature is consciousness, not material extension. The gāthās are in Jain Śaurasenī Prakrit and are traditionally accompanied by Sanskrit and vernacular commentaries that unpack their technical terms.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara Jīva‑kāṇḍa – Guṇasthāna section
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhānta‑Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
मिच्छत्तो सस्सगदो सस्सगदोववरो तदो सम्यग्दंसणो ।
विरदो देसविरदो प्रोयत्तो सुद्धो तदो केवली ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
micchattō sassagado sassagado‑vavaro tado samyag‑damsaṇo;
virado desa‑virado proyatto suddho tado kevalī.
primary_sources.translation:
First is the stage of wrong belief, then the stage of mixed (partial) right belief;
then comes right faith. Renunciation, partial renunciation, effortful conduct, and purity—then the omniscient.
primary_sources.notes: This gāthā schematically presents the progression through the guṇasthānas, highlighting the movement from mithyātva (wrong belief) to samyag‑darśana (right faith) and ultimately kevalī (omniscient). In the full text, Nemichandra elaborates each stage with precise conditions of karmic bondage and spiritual practice. Modern editions often provide tables correlating these stages with specific karmic states, making Gommatasara a key source for technical guṇasthāna study.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara Karma‑kāṇḍa
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhānta‑Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
कम्मं तु पुड्हकं बंधो बंधो तु जिवस्स संजोगो ।
उदयस्स फलं लहइ खवणो मोहो वि तस्स णिव्वत्ति ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
kammaṃ tu puḍhakaṃ bandho bandho tu jivassa saṃjogo;
udayassa phalaṃ lahai khavaṇo moho vi tassa nivvatti.
primary_sources.translation:
Karma is subtle material aggregation; bondage is the soul’s conjunction with it.
Through fruition the soul experiences its results; through destruction, delusion also comes to an end.
primary_sources.notes: This verse encapsulates the Karma‑kāṇḍa’s presentation of karma as material (pudgala) and of bondage as a specific relation between soul and karmic matter. The section proceeds to classify karmas into multiple prakṛtis (types) and to analyze their duration, intensity, and modes of operation. Traditional commentaries and modern critical editions are essential for navigating the highly technical terminology and numerical schemes.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara Jīva‑kāṇḍa – Soul‑classes (Jīva‑samāsa)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhānta‑Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
एगिंदियादि‑पंचिंदिया ठिया तिरिया मनुस्सदेवा च ।
ठिया तिरिया वि निगोडा बहुसंखिया जिवसमासा ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
egindiyādi‑pañcindiyā ṭhiyā tiriyā manus­sadevāc ca;
ṭhiyā tiriyā vi nigodā bahusaṃkhiyā jiva‑samāsā.
primary_sources.translation:
From one‑sensed up to five‑sensed beings, immobile and mobile, humans and gods;
immobile and mobile nigodas—thus are the many soul‑classes.
primary_sources.notes: Here Nemichandra introduces the broad classification of souls by senses, mobility, and special categories like nigoda (group‑souled beings). The full Jīva‑kāṇḍa refines these into detailed numerical classes, which are central to Digambara cosmology and ethics. The presentation is highly schematic, requiring commentary for practical interpretation.

misconceptions.myth: Gommatasara is a simple devotional text meant primarily for lay recitation.
misconceptions.reality: Gommatasara is a highly technical doctrinal compendium, rooted in the Śaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Dhavalā tradition. Its Prakrit verses systematically present complex classifications of souls, karma, and spiritual stages. While laypeople may encounter selected verses or simplified summaries, the full text is intended for advanced scholastic study and is traditionally approached with the aid of commentaries and qualified teachers.

misconceptions.myth: Jīva‑kāṇḍa and Karma‑kāṇḍa are independent works with no structural relationship.
misconceptions.reality: The two sections are conceptually interlinked. Jīva‑kāṇḍa analyzes the soul’s nature and spiritual progression, while Karma‑kāṇḍa explains the karmic mechanisms that condition that progression. The guṇasthāna framework and the soul‑quests (mārgana) provide a shared backbone, and many classifications in Jīva‑kāṇḍa are explicitly correlated with karmic states detailed in Karma‑kāṇḍa.

misconceptions.myth: Because Gommatasara is a ‘summary’, it can replace the study of earlier canonical and commentarial texts.
misconceptions.reality: “Sāra” here means a distilled essence, not a substitute. Gommatasara presupposes familiarity with core Jain doctrines and earlier scriptural material. Traditional study treats it as a gateway into the technical doctrinal tradition, not as a standalone replacement. For a balanced understanding, it is read alongside other texts (such as Śaṭkhaṇḍāgama, Labdhisāra, Trilokasāra) and with guidance from living lineages.

misconceptions.myth: The numerical classifications in Gommatasara are merely symbolic and can be freely reinterpreted.
misconceptions.reality: The numbers and categories in Gommatasara are part of a precise doctrinal system. They encode specific relationships between soul‑types, karmic states, and spiritual stages. While modern scholars may explore symbolic dimensions, traditional interpretation treats these classifications as carefully defined and not arbitrary. Reinterpretation without grounding in the textual and commentarial tradition risks distorting the doctrinal structure.
